districts.label: Union Square
districts.oneLineDistinction: San Francisco’s destination shopping and hotel core
districts.shortDescription: Union Square is San Francisco’s best-known destination retail district, combining major stores, hotels, restaurants and smaller specialty storefronts around a heavily visited downtown setting. Retailers consider it for citywide and visitor exposure rather than primarily neighborhood convenience. Storefront scale and street conditions vary across the wider district, so Powell, Post, Geary and nearby side streets should be evaluated individually.
worthKnowing: Confirm current pedestrian patterns, storefront visibility and block conditions.
accessObservations: Union Square/Market Street station is on the Central Subway.

districts.label: Valencia Street
districts.oneLineDistinction: Independent dining, specialty retail and evening activity
districts.shortDescription: Valencia Street is a recognizable Mission corridor where restaurants, bars, specialty shops, wellness businesses and experiential concepts share fine-grained mixed-use blocks. It draws both neighborhood customers and intentional visitors, with activity extending into evenings. The corridor feels more independent and experience-led than Union Square and more destination-oriented than many daily-needs neighborhood streets.
worthKnowing: Noise, late-hours compatibility, frontage and permitted use require address-level review.

districts.label: Union Street / Cow Hollow
districts.oneLineDistinction: Boutiques, wellness and dining in a neighborhood corridor
districts.shortDescription: Union Street through Cow Hollow is a compact neighborhood and destination corridor associated with boutiques, wellness, beauty, dining and customer-facing services. Its smaller storefronts and planned-visit character distinguish it from Chestnut Street’s broader daily-use mix. Businesses should evaluate the exact block, since the commercial intensity tapers quickly into surrounding residential streets.
worthKnowing: Confirm frontage, accessibility and operating-hour compatibility for the specific address.

districts.label: Chestnut Street
districts.oneLineDistinction: Daily-use retail, dining and services for the Marina
districts.shortDescription: Chestnut Street is a neighborhood-serving corridor with a broad mix of restaurants, fitness, personal services, convenience retail and specialty shops. It supports frequent local visits while also drawing customers from beyond the immediate Marina. Compared with Union Street, the mix generally reads as more daily-use and service-oriented, though individual blocks and storefront formats vary.
worthKnowing: Delivery, parking, ventilation and operating constraints remain property-specific.

districts.label: Fillmore Street
districts.oneLineDistinction: Fashion, dining and services on a walkable neighborhood street
districts.shortDescription: Upper Fillmore combines boutiques, restaurants, wellness and neighborhood services in small mixed-use buildings. The corridor attracts both repeat local customers and planned visits, with a polished but still neighborhood-scaled commercial identity. It offers a more continuous lifestyle-shopping setting than Sacramento Street and a different customer rhythm from the Marina corridors.
worthKnowing: The character and intensity change north and south along Fillmore; verify the exact segment.

districts.label: Sacramento Street
districts.oneLineDistinction: Design, antiques and specialty shopping at neighborhood scale
districts.shortDescription: Sacramento Street is a small linear commercial district in Presidio Heights with boutiques, design and home stores, antiques, personal services and professional offices. It serves nearby residents while also drawing planned visits for specialty shopping. The corridor is quieter and more daytime-oriented than Union Square or Valencia Street, with storefronts interspersed into a low-scale residential setting.
worthKnowing: Evening activity is limited; verify visibility and customer draw for the exact block.

districts.label: Hayes Valley
districts.oneLineDistinction: Design-forward shops, dining and neighborhood destinations
districts.shortDescription: Hayes Valley concentrates independent retail, restaurants, design businesses and personal services along compact mixed-use blocks. It combines neighborhood repeat visits with destination shopping and dining, without the large-format or hotel orientation of Union Square. Smaller storefronts and a strong public-realm identity make it useful for concepts that benefit from a curated neighborhood setting.
worthKnowing: Storefront size, servicing and permitted use vary within older mixed-use buildings.

districts.label: Upper Market / Castro
districts.oneLineDistinction: Transit-oriented services, dining and day-to-evening activity
districts.shortDescription: Upper Market and the Castro combine neighborhood services, restaurants, bars, specialty businesses and customer-facing uses along a strong transit corridor. The district serves local daily needs while also supporting evening and destination activity. It differs from Valencia through its Market Street orientation and from Hayes Valley through a broader service and entertainment mix.
worthKnowing: Hours, sound, ventilation and storefront condition require property-level confirmation.

districts.label: Mission District
districts.oneLineDistinction: Multiple neighborhood corridors with distinct retail rhythms
districts.shortDescription: The broader Mission contains several commercial streets rather than one uniform retail district. Mission Street, Valencia Street, 24th Street and smaller corridors support different combinations of food, services, specialty retail and community-serving businesses. Use the Mission as an orientation layer, then compare the specific corridor: a Valencia storefront can offer a very different setting from Mission Street or a neighborhood-serving block.
worthKnowing: Choose the corridor first; broad neighborhood labels are not enough for site selection.

districts.label: North Beach
districts.oneLineDistinction: Dining, cafes and specialty shops around Columbus Avenue
districts.shortDescription: North Beach is a nonlinear commercial district centered on Columbus Avenue, where restaurants, cafes, bars, specialty retail and neighborhood services share compact mixed-use blocks. It combines strong visitor activity with a continuing local customer base and an active evening economy. Its dining-led, fine-grained character differs from Chinatown’s denser specialty commerce and Union Square’s larger downtown retail setting.
worthKnowing: Visitor intensity, late-hour activity and servicing vary by block.

districts.label: Chinatown
districts.oneLineDistinction: Dense specialty commerce serving community and visitors
districts.shortDescription: Chinatown’s closely spaced storefronts support food, specialty goods, services and culturally specific commerce within one of the city’s most concentrated pedestrian districts. It serves residents and regional customers as well as visitors, so its commercial identity is broader than tourism alone. Small spaces, intense street activity and delivery constraints distinguish it from nearby North Beach and Union Square.
worthKnowing: Servicing, accessibility, ventilation and upper-floor conditions need address-level review.
accessObservations: Chinatown–Rose Pak station is the northern terminus of the Central Subway.

districts.label: Jackson Square
districts.oneLineDistinction: Design showrooms and specialty commerce in historic buildings
districts.shortDescription: Jackson Square’s historic commercial buildings support design showrooms, furnishings, galleries and destination businesses alongside offices. Retail here is typically more planned-visit and specialty-oriented than daily-needs shopping. The intimate building scale and historic streets distinguish it from Union Square’s visitor core and Showplace Square’s larger trade-showroom and production context.
worthKnowing: Street visibility and accessible customer entry vary in older buildings.

districts.label: Financial District
districts.oneLineDistinction: Weekday services and food beneath the office core
districts.shortDescription: Financial District retail is largely shaped by office-worker, commuter and visitor demand. Food, convenience, services and ground-floor commerce sit within a dense office setting rather than a continuous destination-shopping corridor. It can suit weekday-oriented concepts, but block conditions and activity outside business hours differ from Union Square, North Beach or neighborhood retail streets.
worthKnowing: Confirm current foot traffic and daypart demand on the exact block.
accessObservations: Embarcadero and Montgomery BART stations serve the district.

districts.label: SoMa
districts.oneLineDistinction: Event, service and neighborhood retail across varied subareas
districts.shortDescription: SoMa retail is dispersed across very different subareas, including convention and event streets, residential mixed-use blocks, neighborhood services and destination concepts. It should not be read as one continuous shopping district. Retail users may consider it for specific customer generators or emerging mixed-use blocks, but the exact subarea matters more here than the broad SoMa label.
worthKnowing: Validate the immediate block, daypart and surrounding uses before relying on the SoMa label.

districts.label: Mission Bay
districts.oneLineDistinction: Neighborhood services within a newer mixed-use district
districts.shortDescription: Mission Bay retail mainly supports residents, workers, medical visitors and event traffic within a newer planned district. Food, services and convenience uses appear around large blocks and institutional or residential projects rather than a traditional continuous shopping street. It is useful context for operators tied to the district’s daily populations, but less of a citywide retail comparison than Union Square or Valencia Street.
worthKnowing: Confirm customer generators, event dependence and ground-floor visibility at the property.

districts.label: Dogpatch
districts.oneLineDistinction: Neighborhood retail beside historic and production buildings
districts.shortDescription: Dogpatch combines neighborhood restaurants, cafes, services and specialty storefronts with historic residential blocks and nearby production-oriented buildings. Its smaller-scale, local commercial heart differs from Mission Bay’s newer large blocks and Central Waterfront’s protected PDR core. Retail users may value the neighborhood identity, but should not treat the entire waterfront industrial area as a continuous customer-facing district.
worthKnowing: Customer activity and compatible use vary sharply toward the industrial edges.

districts.label: Showplace Square
districts.oneLineDistinction: Trade showrooms and design businesses in former industrial stock
districts.shortDescription: Showplace Square is a specialized design and furnishings district where showrooms, makers, contractors and creative businesses occupy former warehouse and industrial buildings. Retail activity is commonly destination or trade-oriented rather than continuous neighborhood shopping. The larger commercial spaces and production adjacency distinguish it from Jackson Square’s historic boutique scale and Hayes Valley’s pedestrian retail mix.
worthKnowing: Confirm whether a space supports public retail, trade showroom or production use.
